tutorials.problem:
When an integrand contains a product of trigonometric functions, we can often rewrite that product as a sum using the sum and difference formulas. Then, the integral becomes a sum of simpler integrals.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get 

$$
\cos(\alpha-\beta) + \cos(\alpha+\beta) = 2 \cos \alpha \cos \beta.
$$

Now, solving for $\cos \alpha \cos \beta,$ we obtain the following **product-to-sum identity**:

$$
\cos \alpha \cos \beta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\cos(\alpha-\beta)+\cos(\alpha+\beta)\right)
$$

For example, consider the integral

$$
\displaystyle \int \cos(5x)\cos(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the identity above,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{20}\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
